title: Astronaut Spots a Fireball from Space — Was It a Rocket Part?
summary: Have you ever wished on a shooting star? Now imagine seeing one from space — looking down! That's exactly what happened to NASA astronaut Chris Williams. He was on the International Space Station (ISS), a giant lab that zooms around Earth. On April 27, he was in the Cupola, a special room with big windows, waiting to spot a cargo ship bringing supplies. Suddenly, he saw something amazing. "Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," he said. The object grew a tail and then split into many smaller pieces. "It was quite a light show!" Williams thinks it was probably a piece of space junk or an old satellite breaking up as it fell. But here's a cool twist: the fireball might have been part of the rocket that launched the cargo ship he was waiting for! The rocket's upper stage fell back to Earth at just the right time and place. Williams is on his first space trip, living on the ISS with six other astronauts from different countries. They do science experiments and fix things on the station. Next time you look up at the night sky, remember: astronauts are up there, watching the same stars — and sometimes catching a surprise light show!
why_it_matters: Even astronauts get surprised by space light shows, and it reminds us that our old spacecraft parts create beautiful—but risky—fireworks we should work to clean up.

background_read: The International Space Station (a giant laboratory that orbits Earth) has been home to astronauts from many countries since the year 2000.
NASA astronaut Chris Williams is on his first space mission and lives aboard the station with six other crew members.
Fireballs from falling space junk or old satellites happen a few times a year, but seeing one from above is very rare.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA astronaut Chris Williams, on his first space mission.
WHAT: He saw a bright fireball (probably space junk or part of a rocket) break apart while looking down from the ISS Cupola.
WHERE: Over West Africa, through the Cupola's big windows onboard the International Space Station.
WHY: He was waiting to watch a cargo ship arrive, and the fireball might have been the upper stage of the same rocket that launched that cargo ship.

perspectives.description: Chris Williams called it 'quite a light show!' and felt lucky to see such a rare event from a view few people will ever have.
Some experts worry that when space junk breaks up, it creates more dangerous debris that could hit satellites or the space station.
